---
title: "Run a calculation"
---

Every public calculation follows one pattern: build an inputs object with `from_defaults`, pass it to `compute_*`, and read a named-axis series.

```{python}
from qcraft import BaselinePopulationGrowthInputs
from qcraft.api import compute_baseline_population_growth

population_growth = compute_baseline_population_growth(
    BaselinePopulationGrowthInputs.from_defaults(
        country="France",
        demography_scenario="Medium",
    )
)

{
    "axis": population_growth.domain.axes[0].name,
    "first_year": population_growth.domain.axes[0].keys[0],
    "last_year": population_growth.domain.axes[0].keys[-1],
    "value_in_2099": population_growth[2099],
}
```

`from_defaults` fills every leaf on that inputs class from `data.*_DEFAULT`, then applies the keywords you pass. `demography_scenario="Medium"` is explicit here so the call shows the choice; omitting it would have used the same stored default. The labels are the workbook's, and they are case-sensitive: `"Medium"`, `"High"`, and `"Low"`.

## Read the series before you interpret it

Baseline annual series use a `TIME_PERIOD` axis. For population growth that axis runs from 2009 through 2099. Index with the year: `population_growth[2099]`. Fiscal climate series add a `SCENARIO` axis. The scenario labels are `Paris`, `Moderate`, `High`, `Hot`, `Hot adapted`, and `Hot unadapted`. Select one with `.sel(SCENARIO="Paris")`, then index the year on the series that remains.

Look at `result.domain.axes` when a function's horizon is not obvious. Scenario debt, for example, starts in 2028 rather than 2009.

## Set the assumptions that define the baseline

A fiscal result needs the full baseline assumption set. Pass the ones you mean to choose, and leave the rest to the vintage defaults only when those defaults are the assumption you want on the record.

```{python}
from qcraft import BaselineDebtToGdpInputs
from qcraft.api import compute_baseline_debt_to_gdp

baseline_debt = compute_baseline_debt_to_gdp(
    BaselineDebtToGdpInputs.from_defaults(
        country="France",
        demography_scenario="Medium",
        productivity_start=1.0,
        productivity_end=1.1,
        inflation_start=2.0,
        inflation_end=2.0,
        interest_rate_mode="Nominal interest rate",
        real_interest_rate=1.0,
        fiscal_rule_enabled="Yes",
        debt_target=60.0,
    )
)

{
    "debt_to_gdp_2009": baseline_debt[2009],
    "debt_to_gdp_2099": baseline_debt[2099],
}
```

The numbers above are round illustrative assumptions for a reproducible example. The vintage dashboard stores `productivity_start` as `5.0` because its default country is Afghanistan; use that stored value only when it is the assumption you mean to publish.

Units follow the workbook. Productivity and inflation are percentage points (`1.1` means 1.1 percent). `debt_target` is a percent of GDP. `interest_rate_mode` is one of:

- `"Nominal interest rate"`
- `"Interest-growth differential"`
- `"Real interest rate (a)"`

`fiscal_rule_enabled` is `"Yes"` or `"No"`. `real_interest_rate` is part of the inputs object even when the selected mode does not use it as the operative rate; pass the workbook's value, or your own, so the call states it.

Other baseline functions take a subset of these leaves. `compute_baseline_labour_productivity_growth` needs country, demography, and the productivity path. `compute_baseline_gdp_deflator_growth` needs the inflation path. The API reference lists the fields on each `*Inputs` class. `from_defaults` rejects a keyword that class does not have.

## Keep the run reproducible

Store the keyword overrides with the package version and the workbook vintage. Two calls match when they pass the same overrides, because omitted leaves resolve to the same stored defaults. When you publish a table, publish the overrides beside it.
